clinicalPearls: A benign self-limiting neonatal eruption that, unlike erythema toxicum, is typically present at birth and lacks a surrounding erythematous flare.
It evolves through three overlapping stages: fragile superficial pustules, then a collarette of fine scale, then residual hyperpigmented macules.
The pigmented macules can persist for weeks to months and are frequently the only finding by the time the infant is examined.
Unlike erythema toxicum, it commonly involves the palms, soles, chin, forehead, neck and lower back, and shows no age or maturity predilection.
It is disproportionately common in infants with darker, more heavily pigmented skin.
Pustule cytology shows a predominance of neutrophils, in contrast to the eosinophil-rich smear of erythema toxicum neonatorum.
Diagnosis is clinical in a well infant; the pustules are sterile and no treatment is required beyond parental reassurance.
The residual hyperpigmentation represents postinflammatory change and fades completely without intervention.
reference.pathophysiology: Transient neonatal pustular melanosis is a benign, idiopathic neonatal pustular dermatosis. The early pustule is a sterile, subcorneal or intracorneal collection of neutrophils, occasionally with a few eosinophils, without evidence of infection or follicular targeting in the way erythema toxicum shows. As the fragile pustule ruptures, a fine collarette of scale remains, and localised postinflammatory increase in epidermal melanin produces the characteristic hyperpigmented macule. The cause of the initial sterile neutrophilic pustulation is unknown, and it is regarded as a transient reactive phenomenon of newborn skin. The prominence of residual pigmentation in more darkly pigmented infants reflects their greater melanocyte activity and readiness to develop postinflammatory hyperpigmentation.
additionalInvestigations: Wright or Giemsa stain of pustule contents showing predominant neutrophils
Gram stain and bacterial culture to exclude staphylococcal infection
viral swabs and PCR for herpes simplex if vesicular and clinically suspected
potassium hydroxide preparation to exclude candidal pustulosis
septic screen if the neonate is systemically unwell
skin biopsy only in atypical or uncertain cases
clinical follow-up to confirm expected fading of pigmented macules
redFlags: an unwell, febrile or poorly feeding neonate, which is incompatible with this benign diagnosis
grouped vesicles suggesting neonatal herpes simplex infection
positive Gram stain or bacterial culture of pustule contents
linear or blaschkoid vesicular lesions suggesting incontinentia pigmenti
progressive or atypical eruption not following the expected pustule-scale-macule sequence
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is excellent; the pustular and scaling phases resolve within days and the residual hyperpigmented macules fade completely over several weeks to a few months without treatment or scarring.
pitfalls: confusing residual hyperpigmented macules with a pathological pigmentary disorder or bruising
mislabelling the sterile pustules as bacterial infection and treating unnecessarily
failing to distinguish it from erythema toxicum, which is not usually present at birth and is eosinophil-predominant
overlooking neonatal herpes simplex in a vesicular eruption
over-investigating a well infant with classic features
management: Reassurance and observation only, as the eruption is benign and self-resolving without active dermatological treatment

Confirm the sterile nature with a Wright or Giemsa smear showing predominant neutrophils, and exclude infective mimics by Gram stain and culture, herpes simplex PCR and potassium hydroxide preparation before withholding treatment
Routine gentle neonatal skin care, with no need for topical or systemic agents
Counsel parents that the pustular and scaling phases settle within days while residual hyperpigmented macules fade over weeks to months without scarring
Reserve a full septic screen and empirical antimicrobials for the infant who becomes systemically unwell
